title.en: Coyote and the Snake-Monster of the Jocko Valley

region.en: Jocko valley, between Evaro and Ravalli (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 喬科谷，埃瓦羅與拉瓦利之間（象徵定位）

texts.period: Told by Michel Revais; collected by James A. Teit; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Pend d'Oreille Tales, 2. Coyote and the Snake-Monster'

summary.en: A huge rattlesnake-monster occupies the Jocko valley, its tail at Snlpo' near Evaro, its mouth at Skul'io' near Ravalli, its stomach near Jocko: travellers walk into its mouth thinking it a valley, sicken in its stomach and die. Coyote travels through with two long tamarack poles on his shoulder, finds the dying people inside ('You have been swallowed. You are in its stomach now'), plants the poles upright — two tamaracks grow there to-day — and dances under the hanging heart with a sharp arrow-stone dagger fixed on his head until he has killed the monster. Its heart is Butte near Jocko; the props hold the mouth open and the cut tail is the canyon near Evaro, so that people pass through without harm, and the valley is as we see it to-day.
summary.zh: 巨蛇盤踞喬科谷：尾在埃瓦羅附近 Snlpo'，口在拉瓦利附近 Skul'io'，胃近喬科。行人誤以為山谷而入其口，至胃則病亡。郊狼肩扛兩根長落葉松桿入谷，遇垂死之人方知已在蛇胃；遂立桿於地（今彼處仍生兩株落葉松），頭頂利箭石，於懸垂之蛇心下起舞跳擊，直至誅蛇。蛇心即今喬科附近之孤丘；口被撐開、尾被剖開——埃瓦羅附近之峽谷即其割痕。行人從此往來無恙，山谷遂如今貌。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Pend d'Oreille narrative told by Michel Revais (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Landscape etiology for Jocko valley features. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: There was a huge rattlesnake-monster which occupied the Jocko valley. Its tail was at Snlpo' (Come-Out or Emerge), a place near Evaro; and its mouth, at Skul'io', near Ravalli. Its stomach was near Jocko. It swallowed people without their knowing it: they walked into its mouth, and passed on to its stomach, thinking they were going through a valley, and not knowing that they were inside a monster. When they reached the stomach, they became sick, and ere long died.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 115 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: Coyote was travelling with Fox, and reached that district. The people told him of the monster, and he said he would go and kill it. Fox advised him not to go, because he would be killed. Coyote, however, started; and when near the monster's head, he cut two long tamarack-poles, and carried them along on his shoulder, thinking, 'I will use these in case he tries to close his mouth on me.' He passed through the monster's mouth without knowing it. When he reached a place near Arlee, he saw a number of people in all stages of dying, and asked them what they were doing there. 'The monster has killed us,' they answered. 'Where is he? I am looking for him. I don't see anything here to kill you.' — 'You have been swallowed. You are in its stomach now.' Then he placed his poles upright: therefore two tamaracks grow at this place to-day.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 115-116 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: Not very far from there he saw the monster's heart hanging down. Coyote was wearing a sharp arrow-stone fastened upright on his head. He began to dance; and whenever he jumped up, the dagger pierced the heart. Thus he kept on dancing until he had killed the monster. Its heart may still be seen in the shape of Butte, near Jocko. Coyote supported its mouth so that it could not close, and opened its tail; the cut he made may be seen as a canyon near Evaro. Thus Coyote made it possible for people to pass through without hindrance or harm, and the valley was as we see it to-day.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 116 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

title.en: Coyote and Mountain-Sheep: The Rock at Amtkane'
title.zh: 郊狼與大角羊：阿姆特坎之石

region.en: Amtkane', five miles below Missoula (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 阿姆特坎，米蘇拉以南五英里（象徵定位）

texts.period: Told by Michel Revais; collected by James A. Teit; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Pend d'Oreille Tales, 3. Coyote and Mountain-Sheep'

summary.en: At Amtkane', about five miles below Missoula, a large rock stands on the edge of a high cliff and moves when pushed; there lives the Mountain-Ram who kills people — inviting passers-by to push the rock over, then to look over the cliff at the sheep on the rocks below, pushing them over while they look. Coyote, armed, is invited to shoot the sheep, goes to look, and is pushed over and killed; Fox revives him by jumping over him. Returning, Coyote feigns not to see the sheep until Ram leans out over the cliff to point them out — and Coyote shoves him over: 'Had you kept on living and doing this way, you would have exterminated the people.'
summary.zh: 阿姆特坎高地崖邊有一巨石，推之則動。彼處住殺人大角羊：先請過客推石下崖，再請俯瞰崖下石上之羊，趁其觀望推之墜崖。郊狼攜弓矢而來，被請射羊，俯視之際被推落斃命；狐躍其身救活。郊狼復往，佯裝不見羊群；大角羊探身崖外指點，郊狼推其墜崖，曰：『若任爾如此下去，人類將被爾滅絕。』

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Pend d'Oreille narrative (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Coyote was travelling, and came to Amtkane', about five miles below Missoula, where a large rock is standing on the edge of a high cliff; it moves when it is pushed. Here lived the Mountain-Ram who killed people. He invited passers-by to push the rock over the cliff; when they failed, he invited them to look over the cliff at the sheep on the rocks below. Then, while they were looking, he would push them over, and thus kill them. As Coyote was passing, Bighorn shouted to him; Coyote went up and asked him what he wanted. He saw that Coyote was armed, so he said, 'You have bow and arrows. I should like you to shoot those sheep among the rocks below.' Coyote went to look at them; then Bighorn pushed him over, and he was killed on the rocks below.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 116 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: Later Fox came along, and jumped over him. Then Coyote moved, rubbed his eyes, and said, 'I must have slept a long time.' Fox answered, 'You were dead. I told you not to come here.' Coyote said, 'I will be revenged.' Coyote went the same way; and as he was passing, Bighorn shouted as before, and said, 'You have bow and arrows. I want you to shoot these sheep.' Coyote went cautiously to the edge of the cliff, and pretended not to see the sheep; Bighorn pointed them out, but Coyote said he did not see them. Ram leaned out over the cliff to show them to Coyote, and the latter shoved him over and killed him. He said, 'Had you kept on living and doing this way, you would have exterminated the people.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 116 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

title.zh: 郊狼與斯庫庫拉納婦人

region.en: Bitter-Root River bank (symbolic pin near Hamilton)
region.zh: 比特魯特河岸（象徵定位於漢密爾頓附近）

texts.period: Told by Michel Revais; collected by James A. Teit; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Pend d'Oreille Tales, 4. Coyote and the Skukula'na Women'

summary.en: On the Bitter-Root River Coyote hears women dancing in the tall grass singing 'He goes up the ridge' as he crosses, 'He goes down the ridge' as he descends, and joins them; they take him by each hand, dance him toward the river, and drag him up and down until he is drowned — 'It does not matter about clothes in the other world where you are going.' Fox revives him by jumping over his body, and Coyote fires the grass all around them: scorched as they rush through to the river, the women are transformed — 'You shall be Skukula'na, and people shall put you into the fire and eat you' — which is why these fresh-water shellfish appear as if burned on one side.
summary.zh: 比特魯特河畔，郊狼聞高草間眾女歌舞：其上嶺則唱『彼上嶺矣』，下嶺則唱『彼下嶺矣』，遂入其群。眾女左右執其手，舞向河邊，將其拖入水中上下拽曳，直至溺斃——『來世之中，衣衫何足惜哉。』狐躍其屍救活。郊狼復返，縱火焚其四周之草；眾女穿火奔河，皆被灼傷，遂被化為斯庫庫拉納貝：『人將置爾於火中而食之。』故此類貝如今似半邊火烤之狀。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Pend d'Oreille narrative (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Coyote was travelling, and went up Bitter-Root River. There he saw a number of women dancing among tall grass on the bank. He approached, crossing a ridge; he heard them singing, 'He goes up the ridge.' He said, 'They have noticed me. They mean me.' When he went down over the ridge, they sang, 'He goes down the ridge.' Coyote thought, 'They refer to me.' He went down and joined the women. They took him by each hand, and danced with him towards the river. They said, 'We are going into the water.' Coyote said, 'Let me go. My clothes will get wet. I will take them off.' They answered, 'You need not mind. It does not matter about clothes in the other world where you are going.' They took him into the water, and dragged him up and down until he was drowned. They left his body on the bank; and Fox came along, and brought him to life by jumping over him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 116-117 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: Coyote said, 'I shall get even with these women.' He went back, and found them dancing in the same place. He set fire to the grass all around them, and they ran together to get away from the fire; when they saw that it would reach them, they rushed through and ran for the river. As they passed through the fire, they were scorched. Coyote transformed them, saying, 'You shall be Skukula'na, and people shall put you into the fire and eat you.' For this reason these shell-fish appear as if burned on one side.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 117 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

title.en: Coyote and the Elk-Monster of Few-Trees-on-Prairie

region.en: StsE'ltsaltsEle' near Hamilton on the Bitter-Root River (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 比特魯特河漢密爾頓附近 StsE'ltsaltsEle'（象徵定位）

texts.period: Told by Michel Revais; collected by James A. Teit; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Pend d'Oreille Tales, 5. Coyote and Elk'

summary.en: At StsE'ltsaltsEle' (Few-Trees-standing-on-Prairie) near Hamilton, an Elk-Monster lies on a butte commanding the whole prairie, sucking in its breath to swallow every traveller it sees. Coyote has his wife, the Short-Tailed-Mouse, tunnel an underground passage up to the Elk, then emerges right beneath the monster — 'How did you come here? I never saw you. I see everything.' — until Elk believes Coyote's powers are greater than its own. Coyote asks the Elk to attack some people crossing the prairie 'as we do in the world whence I come,' relieves the Elk of its too-large stone dagger 'that will make you tired,' and stabs him to death, cutting out his heart: 'Henceforth you shall be a common elk, and people shall eat you, instead of your eating people.'
summary.zh: 比特魯特河畔漢密爾頓附近之孤丘上臥麋怪，瞰制全原，吸氣即吞所見行旅。郊狼命其妻短尾鼠自丘後掘地道直達麋怪腹下，忽然現身。麋怪大驚：『爾何從至此？吾明察秋毫，未見爾蹤！』遂疑郊狼神通更廣。郊狼唆其出擊原上行人，並借口替其扛那『累人之』巨石匕首而卸其兵，刺之而死，剜其心：『自此爾為凡麋，人食爾，非爾食人。』

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Pend d'Oreille narrative (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Coyote went to StsE'ltsaltsEle' (Few-Trees-standing-on-Prairie), a place near Hamilton on the Bitter-Root River, where an Elk-Monster lived. It lay on a butte there, from which it could see a long distance over the adjoining prairie; nothing could pass over the prairie without being seen by it. When it saw people, it drew in its breath, and they were sucked into its mouth and swallowed; it had thus killed many people.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 117 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: Coyote took his wife, the Short-Tailed-Mouse, with him, and ordered her to dig an underground passage to the Elk. She began to work behind a hill, and tunnelled up to the Elk. Then her husband told her to move camp across the prairie. Coyote went through the passage, and came out right under the Elk-Monster, which was surprised and said, 'How did you come here? I never saw you. I see everything.' Coyote answered, 'I came right across the prairie. You must be blind if you did not see me.' Elk became afraid, for he thought Coyote must have greater powers than he had.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 117 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: Just then Coyote saw the people crossing the prairie. He asked Elk if he saw them, and he answered, 'Yes.' Coyote said, 'Then go and attack them. In the world whence I come we do that. When we see strangers, we go out to attack them and try to take their scalps.' Elk agreed, and Coyote accompanied him. Elk had a large stone dagger. Coyote said, 'That knife will make you tired. It is too large and heavy for you to carry. Let me carry it for you.' Elk gave him the knife, and thus disarmed himself. Then Coyote attacked him, stabbed him to death, and cut out his heart. He said, 'Henceforth you shall be a common elk, and people shall eat you, instead of your eating people.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 117 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

title.en: The Wren and the War on the Sky

region.en: Arrow-chain from the Pend d'Oreille country to the sky (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 自彭德奧雷伊故地直上天際之箭鏈（象徵定位）

texts.period: Told by Michel Revais; collected by James A. Teit; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Pend d'Oreille Tales, 6. The Wren'

summary.en: The Earth people, under Grizzly-Bear their chief, make war on the Sky people; every arrow falls short of the moon until little Wren's shot sticks fast, and the chain of arrows reaching to the ground is climbed — Grizzly-Bear last, whose weight breaks it. Springing for the upper part, he pulls the arrows out at the top and the whole chain falls, stranding the army in the sky. The Earth people defeat the Stars in the first battle but are routed in the second; at the broken ladder each prepares for the fall as best he can: Flying-Squirrel spreads his small robe like wings (hence his wings), Whitefish looks down the hole and puckers his mouth (hence his small puckered mouth), and Sucker jumps unprepared and breaks every bone (hence his bones all through his flesh). At that time there were a number of different animals on earth that are not here now; they were killed in this war and transformed into stars — those we have now are only the survivors.
summary.zh: 地人奉灰熊為酋，征伐天族（星辰）；眾箭皆不及月，唯鷦鷯之箭釘天。箭鏈及地，眾攀之而上，灰熊殿後，體重斷鏈。其躍抓上段，反將頂端之箭拔出，全鏈墜地，征天大軍困於天界。首戰地人勝，再戰為星辰所敗；箭梯已斷，各設法下跳：鼯鼠展小裘如翼，故今有翼；白鮭俯瞰深淵，噘嘴後縮，故其口小而噘；胭脂魚貿然跳下，骨碎遍體，故其骨散於肉中。當時世間尚有多種今已不存之獸，皆歿於此戰，化為星辰——今日之獸，唯其倖存者。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Pend d'Oreille narrative (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Arrow-chain war-on-sky cycle with etiological endings. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: The Earth people wanted to make war on the Sky people. Grizzly-Bear was their chief, and he called all the warriors together. They were told to shoot in turn at the moon (or sky); all did as directed, but their arrows fell short. Only Wren had not shot his arrow. Coyote said, 'He need not shoot. He is too small, and his bow and arrows are too weak.' However, Grizzly-Bear declared that Wren must have his turn. Wren shot his arrow, and it hit the moon (or sky) and stuck fast. Then the others shot their arrows, which stuck each in the nock of the preceding one, until they had made a chain reaching from the sky to the ground. Then all the people climbed up, Grizzly-Bear going last.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 118 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: He was very heavy; and when he was up more than half way, the chain broke by his weight. He made a spring, and caught the part of the chain above him; and this caused the arrows to pull out at the top, where the leading warriors had made a hole to enter the sky. The whole chain fell down, and left the people without means of descending. The Earth people attacked the Sky people (the Stars), and defeated them in the first battle; but the latter soon gathered in such numbers that they far outnumbered the Earth people, and in the next battle routed them, killing a great many — at that time there were a number of different animals on earth that are not here now, but they were killed in this war and transformed into stars: those we have now represent only the survivors of the war.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 118 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: The defeated Earth people ran for the ladder, many being overtaken and killed on the way. When they found the ladder broken, each prepared himself the best way he could, so as not to fall too heavily, and one after another jumped down. Flying-Squirrel was wearing a small robe, which he spread out like wings when he jumped: therefore he has something like wings now, and came down without hurting himself. Whitefish looked down the hole before jumping; when he saw the great depth, he puckered up his mouth and drew back: therefore he has a small puckered mouth at the present day. Sucker jumped down without first preparing himself, and his bones were broken: therefore the sucker's bones are found in all parts of its flesh now.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 118 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

region.zh: 柯達倫故地，愛達荷州（象徵定位）

texts.period: Collected by James A. Teit; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Coeur d'Alene Tales, 1. Conditions in Mythological Times'

summary.en: Long ago the earth was different: much wind and heat, little rain or snow, very dry, thunder frequent and lightning killing many people, and many monsters killing them. Gradually these conditions were changed by Coyote and others, who made transformations beneficial to the people; Coyote also introduced the salmon, made fishing-places, and taught the people many arts. Giants and dwarfs of several kinds inhabited mountains and forests, and Coyote did not transform all of them — some are said to exist at the present day, as do many 'mysteries' both land and water; even many beings that Coyote transformed had not all their evil powers taken from them, and sometimes harm people still.
summary.zh: 上古之世，天地異於今：多風多熱，雨雪稀少，大地乾燥；雷聲頻繁，閃電殺人；怪物橫行。後郊狼與諸賢漸次整治，多行利民之變；郊狼又引鮭魚、闢漁場、授民諸藝。山林之間，巨人與矮人族類繁多，郊狼未及盡化——至今猶有存者；水陸諸『神祕』亦然。即為郊狼所化者，惡力未必盡除，今仍有害人之時。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Coeur d'Alene narrative recorded by Teit (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: A long time ago conditions on the earth were different from what they are now, and people had a hard time to live. There was much wind and heat, and little rain or snow; it was very dry. Some say thunder was frequent, and lightning killed many people. Many monsters lived on earth and killed people. Gradually these conditions were changed by Coyote and others, who made many transformations beneficial to the people. Coyote also introduced the salmon, made fishing-places, and taught the people many arts.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 119 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: Giants and dwarfs of several kinds inhabited some parts of the country, particularly mountains and forests. Coyote did not transform all of them, and some are said to exist at the present day. In the same way some 'mysteries' — both land and water beings — continue to exist. Even many beings that Coyote transformed had not all their evil powers taken from them, and they sometimes harm people at the present day.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 119 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

title.en: Old-One of the Coeur d'Alene: The Chief Who Became the Moon
title.zh: 柯達倫之老者：化月之神

region.zh: 柯達倫故地，愛達荷州（象徵定位）

texts.period: Collected by James A. Teit; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Coeur d'Alene Tales, 2. Old-One'

summary.en: Spoxani'tcElt was a chief and a great man, often appearing in the shape of an old man and helping the people: he travelled about, visited the people, learned what they did, and when he saw that they did not know how to act, he taught them. He did many good, helpful, and kind things, and never fooled people, like Coyote. He was like Christ of the whites, because he did many wonderful things, and always spoke good and did good; at last he ascended to the sky, and was transformed into the moon.
summary.zh: Spoxani'tcElt 乃酋長偉人，常化為老翁濟世：遊歷四方，訪問民眾，察其所為，見其不知者則教之。行善濟人，從不像郊狼那樣捉弄人。彼如白人之基督，多行奇事，言必善，行必善；終升天界，化為明月。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Coeur d'Alene narrative recorded by Teit (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. The informant's Christian analogy is part of the recorded telling. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Spoxani'tcElt was a chief and a great man. He often appeared in the shape of an old man, and helped the people; he travelled about, visited the people, and learned what they did. When he saw that they did not know how to act, he taught them. He did many good, helpful, and kind things, and never fooled people, like Coyote. He was like Christ of the whites, because he did many wonderful things, and always spoke good and did good. At last he ascended to the sky, and was transformed into the moon.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 119-120 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

title.en: Coyote's Son: The Tree to the Sky and the Spider Rope
title.zh: 郊狼之子：通天樹與蜘蛛索

region.en: Eagle tree grown to the sky; spider country (symbolic pin at Coeur d'Alene)
region.zh: 通天之鷹樹與蜘蛛之國（象徵定位於柯達倫）

texts.period: Collected by James A. Teit; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Coeur d'Alene Tales, 3. Coyote's Son'

summary.en: Jealous of his son To'rtorsEmstEm, Coyote lures him to climb for an eagle's nest, blinking his eyes all the while — 'I am afraid some dust may get into my eyes and blind me' — each blink making the tree grow taller until it reaches the sky. In the new country the youth finds two Spider people quarrelling over Indian-hemp; deaf to beads and necklaces, they listen at once to two fathoms of hemp apiece, and let him down to earth by a rope in a basket — stop four times, turn over, not rise, tug the rope when he hears the grass of his own country. Home again, he found his father and killed him.
summary.zh: 郊狼妒其子 To'rtorsEmstEm，誘其攀樹取鷹雛；攀高之際，郊狼頻頻眨眼——『怕灰塵入眼』——每眨一次，樹便長高一截，直至通天。其子在天上新國遇蜘蛛二人爭論印第安大麻之爭；珠鏈項圈皆不動心，唯各得兩庹大麻方止爭，遂以繩繫籃縋其下凡——途中四停，每停須翻轉不可上升；聞故鄉草聲即可出籃。既歸，尋得其父而殺之。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Coeur d'Alene narrative recorded by Teit (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Sky-ascent cycle (cf. Thompson name parallels noted by Teit). Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Coyote was jealous of his son To'rtorsEmstEm, and wanted to get rid of him. He told him that he knew of an eagle's nest in a tree, and induced him to go there with him and climb for it, saying that he wanted the young eagles for their tail-feathers. When up quite high, the youth looked down and saw his father blinking his eyes. 'Why are you doing that, father?' Coyote answered, 'I am afraid some dust may get into my eyes and blind me.' By blinking his eyes Coyote made the tree grow tall: each time he blinked, the tree grew. To'rtorsEmstEm looked down again, and saw his father still looking up and blinking his eyes. The tree grew up until it reached the sky, and there To'rtorsEmstEm found himself in a new country.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 120 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: He travelled about, and at last came to a lodge where he heard talking: two Spider people inside were quarrelling about Indian-hemp, one saying it grew one way and belonged to him, the other saying it grew another way and belonged to him. 'Grandchildren, I want you to take me back to my country,' he addressed them, but they paid no attention; beads and necklaces were offered, and still no heed. Then he offered them each two fathoms of Indian-hemp, and at once they ceased their quarrelling and became attentive, promising to let him down to his country by a rope. They put him into a basket with the rope fastened to it: 'You will stop four times on your way down. You must not rise, but turn over; then the basket will proceed. When the basket stops the fourth time, you will be on the earth; and when you hear the grass, you will know that you are in your own country. Then step out of the basket and tug the rope, and we will pull it up.' He did as directed, and they pulled it up. To'rtorsEmstEm went home, found his father, and killed him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 120-121 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

title.en: Coyote and the Sun: The Stolen Heart

region.en: Drinking-place of the Sun at the edge of the earth (symbolic pin at Coeur d'Alene)
region.zh: 大地邊界太陽飲水處（象徵定位於柯達倫）

texts.period: Collected by James A. Teit; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Coeur d'Alene Tales, 4. Coyote and the Sun'

summary.en: The Sun had killed Coyote's children, and Coyote resolved on revenge: lying in wait, he kills the Sun as it comes down from the sky to drink, and cuts out its heart — whereupon the earth becomes totally dark. Carrying the heart home, each step he takes he treads on the Sun (or Sun's body), can make no progress, and at last, exhausted, places the heart back on the Sun; the Sun comes to life at once, and there is light over the world as before.
summary.zh: 太陽殺郊狼諸子，郊狼誓報：伏於太陽下凡飲水之處，殺之剜心。剎那間天地全黑。郊狼攜心歸家，然而每跨一步，必踏太陽之軀，寸步難行；力竭之餘，將心放回太陽之身。太陽頃刻復生，世界重見光明。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Coeur d'Alene narrative recorded by Teit (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Sun-capture cluster. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: The Sun had killed Coyote's children, and Coyote resolved to take revenge. He lay in wait; and when the Sun came down from the sky to drink, he killed him and cut out his heart. At once the earth became totally dark. Coyote tried to go home carrying Sun's heart; but each time he made a step, he trod on the Sun (or Sun's body). He could make no progress; and at last he was exhausted, and placed the heart on the Sun. The latter at once came to life, and there was light over the world, as before.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 121 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

title.en: Coyote Introduces Salmon to the Coeur d'Alene

region.en: Dam of the four women on the Columbia River (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 哥倫比亞河四女之壩（象徵定位）

texts.period: Collected by James A. Teit; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Coeur d'Alene Tales, 5. Coyote introduces Salmon'

summary.en: Four women on the Columbia River hold the salmon back from the interior with a dam, attacking and eating whoever comes near. Coyote changes himself into a board, floats down to the dam, becomes a baby, and is taken in to be reared by the husbandless, childless women; slipping out 'for a drink,' he undermines the dam for three days, and on the fourth, found out, he tears out the last pieces under their clubs — his armor protecting him — and leaps to the opposite bank as the water bursts through. Great numbers of salmon ascend the river, and Coyote conducts them up the streams, introducing them in many places; thus he benefited his people, for before this the Indian tribes of the interior had no salmon.
summary.zh: 哥倫比亞河上四女築壩攔鮭，近者皆遭其噬。郊狼化為木板漂流至壩，再化為嬰兒，被無夫無子之四女拾回收養。借口出壩飲水，三度潛掘壩基；第四日事發，四女持棒亂擊其手足，然其有甲護身。郊狼拆去最後幾塊，水決而出，他躍至對岸。群鮭上溯，郊狼引之溯流而上，遍置於諸水——故內陸諸族自此始得鮭魚，民受其惠。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Coeur d'Alene narrative recorded by Teit (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Salmon-liberation cycle, Coeur d'Alene version. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Four women who lived on the Columbia River had a dam which held the salmon from ascending to the interior. Whoever came near them was attacked and eaten by them. Coyote heard of them and their salmon, and resolved to go and break the dam. He changed himself into a board, and floated down the stream until he reached the dam; then he changed himself into a baby. The women were out on the dam catching salmon; they saw him, and, thinking that he was a baby, said they would take him to their house and rear him as their son, for they were glad to have a child, having neither husbands nor children.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 121 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: After Coyote had been with them a while, he wanted to go out on the dam to have a drink, and they gave their permission. He began to undermine and break up the dam, but did not stay very long for fear of arousing their suspicions; he did so on three days, and the dam was nearly broken through. On the fourth day he stayed longer than usual, and the women went to see what was the matter. When they came to the river-bank and looked down, they saw Coyote tearing down their dam. They rushed at him and clubbed him over hands and arms, but he was protected by armor. Coyote tore out the last pieces; now the water rushed through the break, and Coyote jumped to the opposite side.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 121 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: Most of the dam was carried away, and great numbers of salmon ascended the river. Coyote conducted them up the streams, introducing them in many places; thus Coyote benefited his people, for before this the Indian tribes of the interior had no salmon.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 121 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

title.en: Coyote and Wewel'tc: The Big-Mouthed Pass Monster
title.zh: 郊狼與韋韋爾茨：隘口巨口怪

region.en: Passes between the hills of the Coeur d'Alene country (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 柯達倫故地山隘（象徵定位）

texts.period: Collected by James A. Teit; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Coeur d'Alene Tales, 6. Coyote and Wewel'tc'

summary.en: A monster used to set his head in the gaps between hills with his mouth wide open; people crossing the hills walked into his mouth and on into his stomach without noticing it, and many were thus swallowed and eaten. 'Oh, he is nothing! I shall go and kill him,' said Coyote, taking a long tamarack pole; a voice at the pass called, 'Where are you going, Coyote?' — and when Coyote answered that he was seeking the man-eating monster, 'Don't kill him!' — 'Well, if you promise not to eat people, I will spare you.' The monster promised, and Coyote transformed him into the wewel'kc-bird: 'You shall be a bird with a big mouth, but shall not be able to eat people any more.'
summary.zh: 有怪居於山隘，張巨口以待：越山人不知不覺步入其口，直達其胃，多有被吞者。郊狼聞之曰：『區區小怪！吾往誅之。』携長落葉松桿上山；臨隘有聲問：『郊狼欲往何處？』郊狼答：『尋食人之怪。』聲曰：『勿殺之！』郊狼曰：『若允諾不復食人，可留汝命。』怪允諾。郊狼遂化其為韋韋爾茨鳥：『自此爾為大口之鳥，不得再食人。』

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Coeur d'Alene narrative recorded by Teit (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: There was a monster who used to go to the passes between hills, and place his head in the gap with his mouth wide open. People crossing the hills walked into his mouth, and on into his stomach, without noticing it; thus he had swallowed and eaten many people. Coyote heard of this monster, and said, 'Oh, he is nothing! I shall go and kill him.' He took a long pole of tamarack, and went up the hills. As he neared a pass, he heard a voice saying, 'Where are you going, Coyote?' He answered, 'I am seeking the monster who eats men. I will find him, and learn if he eats men. I do, but he does not.' Coyote went on. Again the voice said, 'Don't kill him!' Coyote answered, 'Well, if you promise not to eat people, I will spare you.' The monster promised. Then Coyote transformed him into the wewel'kc-bird, saying, 'You shall be a bird with a big mouth, but shall not be able to eat people any more.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 121-122 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

region.en: Mouth of the Palouse River (symbolic pin)

texts.period: Collected by James A. Teit; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Coeur d'Alene Tales, 7. Division of the Cannibal's Body'

summary.en: A large monster around the mouth of the Palouse River had killed many people; a man gifted with magic attacked him in his house, and after a long combat the monster died. The victor threw his ornaments and clothing about, cut up the body, and threw a piece to each tribe: the head down the river to the Wishram (big heads), the scalp to the Crows (long hair), the ribs and chest to the Nez Perce (large-bodied), the legs to the Blackfeet (a tall people), the heart to the Coeur d'Alene — noted ever after as brave fighters of cruel disposition — and pieces to the Salish, the Columbias and all the rest. Two tribes had been forgotten; finding no scraps, he wiped his knife with a bunch of grass and threw the knife to one tribe, probably the Thompson, and the grass to the SEntatuu'li of Hangman's Creek, Spokane — who therefore have never been a numerous people.
summary.zh: 帕盧斯河口巨魔殺人無算；有神通者入其宅與之鬥，久戰而誅之。勝者散其飾物衣物，剖其屍分擲諸族：頭擲下游之威什拉姆人——故其頭大；髮皮擲烏鴉——故其髮長；肋胸擲內茲珀斯人——故其軀偉；腿擲黑腳人——故其身高；心擲柯達倫人——故其族以勇戰剛烈著稱；餘肉分與薩利什、哥倫比亞等各族。尚有二族被遺忘；遍尋無餘屑，乃以草拭刀，擲刀與一族（或即湯普森人），擲草與斯波坎漢人溪之 SEntatuu'li——故其族人丁始終不旺。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Coeur d'Alene narrative recorded by Teit (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Dismemberment ethnogony parallel (Ymir/Pangu/Purusha cluster). Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Once a large monster inhabited the country around the mouth of the Palouse River. He had killed many people. Coyote, or some other man gifted with magic, made up his mind to rid the country of this evil being. He went to his house and attacked him; the combat lasted a long time, and ended with the monster's death. Then the victor took off the ornaments and clothing of his victim, and threw them about; then he cut up the body, and threw a piece to each tribe.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 122 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: He threw the head down the river to the Wishram: therefore they now have big heads. He threw the scalp to the Crows, for they have long hair. He cut out the ribs and chest and threw them to the Nez Perce: therefore they are large-bodied. He threw the legs to the Blackfeet: therefore they are a tall people. He threw the heart to the Coeur d'Alene: therefore they became noted as brave fighters, and of cruel disposition. Thus he threw pieces to all the tribes — to the Salish, to the Columbias, and so on.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 122 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: He thought every one had received a piece; then he remembered that two tribes had been forgotten. He looked around, but could find no scraps to give them. He took his knife, and, after wiping it with a bunch of grass, threw it to one tribe, probably the Thompson; he threw the grass to the SEntatuu'li. Therefore the latter have never been a numerous people.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 122 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

title.en: The Sun and the Moon: Choosing the Carriers

region.en: Sky above the Coeur d'Alene country (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 柯達倫故地上空（象徵定位）

texts.period: Collected by James A. Teit; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Coeur d'Alene Tales, 8. The Sun and the Moon'

summary.en: The people could not manage the sun: carriers went too near — killing many by heat — too far, or zigzag, and were deposed one after another. Robin was elected, but soon came so near that the people fled into the water and stayed immersed all day, until even the water got hot; then a one-eyed man, .s.tsakozaltsasa'-xkEn, was chosen, who keeps a straight and even course and carries the sun yet. The moon fared as badly: Coyote offered to carry it, and in his nightly travels called out people's names and told what they were doing — loudly, when he saw married people together — until the annoyed people deposed him and asked Spoxani'tcElt (Old-One) to take his place; he did his work perfectly, and carries the moon yet.
summary.zh: 世人苦於日行無度：擔日者或太近灼人、或太遠失明、或曲行無定，相繼被廢。眾乃選知更鳥擔日，然其不久便贴近大地，人皆整日泡於水中，連水都燒熱了。於是改選獨眼人 .s.tsakozaltsasa'-xkEn，其行路平直有度，至今擔日。月亦然：郊狼自薦，夜行時高唱人名，揭露各人所為——見夫婦同寢，更是聲震四野——眾人不堪其擾，遂廢之，請老者 Spoxani'tcElt 代之；其行事盡善，至今擔月。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Coeur d'Alene narrative recorded by Teit (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: The people had trouble with the sun. They could not manage to make it go right. They tried different people to carry it, but they did not do it properly, and the people deposed them: most of them did not carry it at the right distance from the earth; some went in a zigzag course, sometimes too far away, then too near; those who carried it too near killed many people by the heat. Then the people chose Robin to carry the sun, for they could not do without heat and light; he had to travel only in the daytime, for at night the moon was carried instead. Robin carried the sun, but soon came so near to the earth that the people had to flee to the water and keep themselves immersed all day; soon even the water got hot. Therefore they deposed Robin, and elected a one-eyed man called .s.tsakozaltsasa'-xkEn in his stead. This man was able to keep a straight and even course in the sky, and carries the sun yet.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 123 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: At the same time the people had trouble with the moon. They had tried several people to carry it, but none of them had done it properly. Coyote had offered to carry it, but the people did not trust him; at last they thought they would try him. In his nightly travels he called out people's names, and told what they were doing. When he saw married people together, he called out their names loudly, so that every one could hear, and told what they were doing. This so much annoyed the people that they deposed him, and asked Spoxani'tcElt to take his place. The latter did his work perfectly, and carries the moon yet.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 123 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

region.en: Feast of the moon at Spoxani'tcElt's house (symbolic pin at Coeur d'Alene)
region.zh: 老者家中月神之宴（象徵定位於柯達倫）

texts.period: Collected by James A. Teit; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Coeur d'Alene Tales, 9. Toad and the Moon'

summary.en: After Spoxani'tcElt took up the duty of being moon, he invited the people to a feast, and the house was soon crowded. Toad came along, found it full, was told 'There is no place to sit,' went home angry, and made a heavy rain that penetrated everything, putting out lights and fires. Driven from tent to tent, under canoes, the people followed a light to Toad's house, dry inside, and crowded in; then Toad jumped on Spoxani'tcElt's face and sat there, and at once the rain stopped. The people tried to pull Toad off his face and did not succeed — the marks of Toad may still be seen on the moon.
summary.zh: 老者既擔月，設宴款眾；屋中人滿。蟾蜍至，問座處，答曰：『無隙可坐。』蟾怒歸，召大雨，透屋滅燈熄火。眾人倉皇避雨，自帳至舟底皆滲漏；見一光，趨之——乃蟾蜍之屋，內中乾爽——遂擠入。蟾蜍一躍而上，坐在老者面上，雨立止。眾欲拽之不下——月面上蟾蜍之影，至今猶在。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Coeur d'Alene narrative recorded by Teit (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: After Spoxani'tcElt had taken up the duty of being moon, he invited the people to a feast; so many people went to the feast that his house was soon crowded. Toad came along, and found the house full. She asked where she was to sit, and he answered, 'There is no place to sit.' She became angry, and returned to her own house; then she made a heavy rain, which penetrated everything and put out lights and fires.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 123 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: As more people arrived, they crowded inside, saying, 'Chief, where are we to sit? It is wet outside.' At last, as the rain came pouring through the roof of the house, all the people cried aloud, 'Chief, where are we to sit? Where can we go to be out of the rain?' They went from tent to tent, but it rained through them all; they went under canoes, but it rained through them also. Finally they saw a light, and went to it: it was in Toad's house, and inside it was quite dry. They crowded in. Then Toad jumped on Spoxani'tcElt's face, and sat there; at once the rain stopped. The people tried to pull Toad off his face, but did not succeed. The marks of Toad may still be seen on the moon.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 123-124 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

region.en: Windy plains of the Coeur d'Alene country (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 柯達倫故地多風之原（象徵定位）

texts.period: Collected by James A. Teit; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Coeur d'Alene Tales, 10. The Wind'

summary.en: The wind used to blow hard all the time; the people had no peace, and many were hurt. Coyote made a snare and tried to catch the Wind, but Wind always passed through it; he made his snare smaller and smaller, and finally caught the Wind. Then he took away its power of hurting the people, and released it — since then the wind has been as we know it to-day.
summary.zh: 古時終日狂風，民無寧日，多受其害。郊狼結網捕風，風屢穿網而過；網愈結愈小，終於縛住風。郊狼收其害人之力，然後放風歸山——故今日之風，溫馴如常。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Coeur d'Alene narrative recorded by Teit (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: The wind used to blow hard all the time. The people had no peace, and many were hurt. Then Coyote made a snare and tried to catch the Wind, but Wind always passed through his snare. He made his snare smaller and smaller, and finally caught the Wind. Then he took away his power of hurting the people, and released it. Since then the wind has been as we know it to-day.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 124 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

region.en: Between the far north and the south, wind-bag countries (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南北風囊之國之間（象徵定位）

texts.period: Collected by James A. Teit; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Coeur d'Alene Tales, 11. The Hot and Cold Winds'

summary.en: Formerly the Earth was vexed with hot and cold winds caused by the Wind people striving with each other: the Cold-Wind people in the far north pressed the bag in which they kept the wind, and a cold wind rushed south; the Hot-Wind people, becoming cold, pressed their own wind-bag, and a hot wind rushed north, making the Cold-Wind people sick, who pressed their bag again. Thus the conflict continued constantly between the two, until some one made peace between these people, or curtailed their powers — therefore cold and warm winds blow as they do now.
summary.zh: 上古之世，風族相爭，冷熱之風肆虐大地。寒風族居極北，按其風囊，寒風南掃；熱風族覺冷，急按己囊，熱風北襲，寒族遂病，復按其囊。兩族相持不休。後有賢者為之和解，或削其力——故今之冷暖二風，各行其道，不復相殘。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Coeur d'Alene narrative recorded by Teit (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Formerly the Earth was vexed with hot and cold winds, caused by the Wind people, who were striving with each other. The Cold-Wind people lived in the far north, and the Hot-Wind people in the south. The Cold-Wind people would press the bag in which they kept the wind in their house, and immediately a cold wind would rush out, and blow over the country. When it reached the Hot-Wind people, they became cold, and at once pressed their wind-bag, and a hot wind rushed north. When it reached the Cold-Wind people, they became sick, and they pressed their bag. Thus the conflict continued constantly between the two. Some one made peace between these people, or curtailed their powers; therefore cold and warm winds blow as they do now.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 124 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

title.en: Heat and Cold: The Two Brothers

region.en: South journey of Heat; winter of Cold (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 熱神南遊，寒神肆虐（象徵定位）

texts.period: Collected by James A. Teit; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Coeur d'Alene Tales, 12. Heat and Cold'

summary.en: Heat and Cold were two brothers, the former good-looking and the latter ugly. One fall Heat travelled south, and then Cold made up his mind to kill the people: he made the weather so cold that most of them died. Heat hurried back to save them, and made the weather so hot that he killed his brother, and the frost and ice and snow he had made disappeared. It was then ordained that cold should not prevail long at a time, and should always be driven away by heat — we see the killing of Cold by his brother every spring.
summary.zh: 熱與寒本為兄弟，兄俊弟陋。一年秋天，熱神南遊；寒神趁機肆虐，天寒地凍，民多凍斃。熱神聞訊急返，天氣頓熱，寒神竟被熱死，冰雪霜霜俱消。自此天命：寒不得久居，必為熱所驅——每年春天，我們都看見兄弟殺寒的這一幕。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Coeur d'Alene narrative recorded by Teit (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Season-cycle myth. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Heat and Cold were two brothers, the former good-looking, and the latter ugly. One fall Heat travelled south, and then Cold made up his mind to kill the people: he made the weather so cold that most of the people died. Heat hurried back to save them, and made the weather so hot that he killed his brother, and the frost and ice and snow which he had made disappeared. It was then ordained that cold should not prevail long at a time, and should always be driven away by heat. We see the killing of Cold by his brother every spring.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 124 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

region.en: House of Thunder in the high mountains (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 高山雷神之居（象徵定位）

texts.period: Collected by James A. Teit; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Coeur d'Alene Tales, 13. Thunder'

summary.en: Thunder used to kill many people by shooting down large arrow-stones; when he wanted rain, he sang. A man went to his house in the high mountains and tore up his dress, which was made of feathers; after this the thunder was only able to thunder when it was about to rain, and could not kill people any more.
summary.zh: 雷神常擲大箭石殺人；欲雨則歌。一人上高山雷神之居，撕其羽衣。自此雷唯在欲雨之時作聲，再不能殺人。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Coeur d'Alene narrative recorded by Teit (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Thunder used to kill many people by shooting down large arrow-stones. When he wanted rain, he sang. A man went to his house in the high mountains, and tore up his dress, which was made of feathers. After this the thunder was only able to thunder when it was about to rain, and could not kill people any more.
